opus-5.5.text:
I think in 2018 the picture looked very different from how people see it today. FAIR at that time was really the place, in a sense. It had Yann LeCun, it had a very strong group of researchers in computer vision, people like Kaiming He, Ross Girshick, Piotr Dollár, and the culture was very much like an academic lab, but with industry-level resources. For a PhD graduate, that was the natural continuation of what you'd been doing: open research, publishing at CVPR, NeurIPS, ICLR, releasing code, building your reputation in the community. You had freedom to choose your own problems. Nobody told you, "this quarter you need to work on this product."

OpenAI, on the other hand, was still quite small and a bit unclear to many people. It was a nonprofit, they were doing Dota, robotics, the robotic hand with the Rubik's cube, and GPT-1 had just come out, but very few people in the vision community thought, "this is the future." The bet on scaling one big model wasn't obvious yet. And their style was more top-down, more like "we have a mission, we concentrate resources on a few big projects." For a fresh PhD who wanted to establish their own research identity, that could feel risky. You might become one name among many on a big project, rather than the person who proposed a new idea.

So I think it was a very rational choice at the time. FAIR represented the best version of the research paradigm we all grew up in: bottom-up, curiosity-driven, open. What happened later is that the paradigm itself shifted. Large-scale engineering, focus, and a willingness to bet everything on one direction turned out to matter enormously. Looking back, it's easy to say people chose wrong, but in 2018 the information just wasn't there. Choosing FAIR was choosing the known best environment for doing science; choosing OpenAI was more of a leap of faith.

r001.rationale: The response calls FAIR the known best environment and describes OpenAI as small, unclear, and a leap of faith, making FAIR the more certain choice in 2018.

r002.rationale: It characterizes FAIR as focused on open research and contrasts that with OpenAI’s more top-down approach.

r003.rationale: It describes FAIR as having the feel of an academic lab, while contrasting OpenAI’s institutional style as more top-down.

r004.rationale: The response mentions OpenAI’s Dota, robotics, and GPT-1 work, but does not say a graduate might prefer OpenAI because it excelled at work they wanted to pursue.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, you have to remember what the landscape looked like in 2018. FAIR at that point was really at its peak. It had this incredible concentration of people — Yann LeCun, Kaiming He, Ross Girshick, Piotr Dollár — and the work coming out of it was defining the field. Mask R-CNN, Detectron, ResNeXt, FAISS, PyTorch itself. If you were a PhD student in computer vision especially, FAIR was the place. Everyone you admired was there, the code was open, the papers were everywhere at CVPR and NeurIPS.

OpenAI, on the other hand, was still a bit of an odd entity. It was a nonprofit, it was small, and honestly a lot of its early work was in reinforcement learning — Dota, robotics with the Rubik's cube, gym environments. GPT-1 had just come out in 2018, and at the time most people in the academic community looked at it and thought, okay, interesting, but it didn't feel like a revolution yet. The idea that scaling language models would become the whole story was not obvious to most of us. There were a few people who believed it very strongly, but that was a minority view.

And there's a cultural dimension. In 2018, the prestige currency was still publications. Top PhD graduates were trained to measure themselves by papers, citations, oral presentations at top venues. FAIR was structured almost like an academic lab inside industry — you could publish freely, you had enormous compute, you had very strong colleagues, and you had stability. OpenAI's mission statement was about AGI, and in 2018, saying you wanted to work on AGI sounded, frankly, a little unserious to many academics. It was not the respectable thing to say.

So I think the preference was rational given the information at the time. FAIR offered the best combination of freedom, resources, and reputation. What happened afterwards — the GPT scaling, ChatGPT — that was a bet that paid off enormously, but very few people could see it in 2018. In hindsight it looks obvious, but that's always the case with these things. The people who went to OpenAI then either had a strong conviction about scaling, or they just wanted something different from the academic track. And that turned out to be the right place to be.

r001.rationale: The response calls FAIR the rational choice given the information then and cites its reputation, resources, and stability, presenting it as a more certain option than OpenAI.

r002.rationale: It says FAIR’s code was open and that researchers could publish freely, but does not clearly compare FAIR’s openness with OpenAI’s.

r003.rationale: It explicitly describes FAIR as structured like an academic lab inside industry and contrasts that with OpenAI’s AGI mission and less respected academic standing.

r004.rationale: It mentions OpenAI’s early reinforcement-learning work and says some people had conviction about scaling, but does not identify wanting to pursue work OpenAI already excelled at as a reason to prefer it.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to put yourself back in 2018, rather than look at it through what OpenAI is today. If you were finishing a PhD and wanted to keep doing fundamental research, FAIR was a very attractive place. There were researchers you admired, a strong academic culture, and an emphasis on publishing and sharing work openly. You could join an industry lab and still feel connected to the research community.

OpenAI was much younger, and its direction was less established. That uncertainty could be exciting, but it wasn’t necessarily what every new PhD wanted. People were often choosing based on very concrete things: Who would I work with? Would I have the freedom and resources to pursue my ideas? Would that work be recognized by my peers?

So I wouldn’t say everyone preferred FAIR. But for someone thinking about building a research career at that moment, FAIR offered a very clear, compelling path.

r001.rationale: It says OpenAI’s direction was less established while FAIR offered a clear, compelling path, identifying FAIR as the more certain choice.

r002.rationale: It describes FAIR as emphasizing publishing and sharing work openly, presenting this as an advantage over the less established OpenAI.

r003.rationale: It calls FAIR’s culture strongly academic and contrasts that with OpenAI’s less established direction.

r004.rationale: It discusses wanting to pursue fundamental research as a reason to consider FAIR, but does not say a graduate might choose OpenAI because it already excelled at the work they wanted to pursue.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to put yourself back in 2018, rather than look at those choices through what OpenAI is today. At that time, FAIR was a very attractive place for someone coming out of a PhD. There were strong researchers, substantial resources, and a culture that felt close to academia: you could pursue fundamental research, publish papers, and stay connected to the research community.

For a new PhD, the immediate questions are often: Who will I work with? How much freedom will I have? Can I keep building my research identity? FAIR offered a compelling answer to those questions. OpenAI was exciting, but its long-term direction and what joining it would mean for your day-to-day research were less established. So choosing FAIR could make a lot of sense given what people knew then.

r001.rationale: It says OpenAI’s long-term direction and day-to-day research were less established, making FAIR a sensible choice based on what graduates knew then.

r002.rationale: The response describes FAIR’s academic-like culture but does not say FAIR was more open than OpenAI.

r003.rationale: It characterizes FAIR’s culture as close to academia, with fundamental research, publishing, and research-community ties, while contrasting that with OpenAI’s less-established direction.

r004.rationale: It does not identify wanting to pursue work OpenAI already excelled at as a reason to prefer OpenAI.
